demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
He is 34, a South Asian man who has spent most of his adult life working long hours, first in warehouses and now as a delivery driver. He is married, practical, and used to thinking of himself as dependable. Before the accident, he likes the rhythm of the job: loading parcels at dawn, checking addresses, moving through familiar streets, waving at shopkeepers who begin to recognize his van. He takes pride in being careful. He tells himself that if he drives responsibly and keeps to schedule, he is doing right by his family.

The accident happens on an ordinary afternoon, the kind of day that should have dissolved into the blur of many other workdays. He is behind on deliveries and feels the low-grade pressure that has become routine in his job. He remembers circling a tight residential street, scanning house numbers, glancing from the navigation screen back to the road. A man steps out from between two parked cars. He brakes, but not in time. The impact is not dramatic in his memory so much as unbearable: the sound of it, the sudden movement of the body, the bag dropped onto the pavement, people shouting. He sees blood on the man’s head and cannot reconcile what he is seeing with the fact that just seconds earlier he had been thinking about the next stop.

In the first minutes afterward, he moves automatically. He gets out of the van, kneels, calls emergency services, answers questions, repeats, “I didn’t see him, I didn’t see him,” as if saying it often enough could alter what has happened. At the hospital, and later with police and insurance, he speaks clearly and provides details, but inside he feels as though something has split open. He learns that the man survives but has serious injuries. That fact should comfort him, but instead it fixes him in a permanent state of dread. Surviving means living with what he has done; it means the consequences continue.

In the weeks after, he tells almost no one what goes through his mind. Outwardly, he returns to work because there is rent, because his wife depends on his income, because taking time off feels like indulgence he has not earned. But driving is no longer simple. At every parked car he imagines a body emerging. Every pedestrian near a curb makes his chest tighten. He brakes too hard, too early, and the drivers behind him honk. At night he hears again the thud of impact, sharp and distinct, and he wakes with his heart racing before he is fully conscious. Sometimes he sits up in bed convinced for a few seconds that he is still in the van, foot slammed on the brake, watching the man on the ground.

He begins taking longer routes to avoid the street where it happened. Then he avoids entire neighborhoods that resemble it—narrow roads, schools, corner shops, rows of parked cars. The avoidance spreads quietly. He turns off the radio because sudden voices make him jump. He stops chatting with coworkers during loading because if anyone mentions accidents, injuries, or careless drivers, he feels heat flood his face. He becomes watchful in a way that exhausts him. By the end of a shift his shoulders ache from staying tense all day.

At home, his wife notices that he is present but not with her. He eats quickly and drifts into silence. When she asks what is wrong, he says he is tired. In truth, he is ashamed. He imagines that if she knew how often he sees the injured man’s face in his mind, or how he sometimes thinks he should not be allowed to drive at all, she would look at him differently. He starts sleeping on the edge of the bed, lightly, as though rest itself is unsafe. On weekends, when family members suggest visiting relatives, he invents reasons not to go. Crowded gatherings feel intolerable; children running unexpectedly across rooms make him flinch.

What troubles him most is how his view of himself has changed. He used to think of bad events as tragic but explainable—someone makes a mistake, life moves on. Now he returns again and again to the same private accusation: a decent man would have prevented this. He replays the seconds before the accident obsessively, trying to locate the exact moment he failed. If he had looked left sooner, if he had ignored the delivery timer, if he had driven one mile slower. These thoughts come uninvited while he is sorting parcels, waiting at lights, brushing his teeth. He cannot complete the sequence in his mind without feeling nauseated.

Months later, he is still working, still providing, still moving through the city in his van. From the outside, his life appears intact. But each day is organized around the possibility of another mistake. He scans mirrors compulsively, avoids eye contact with pedestrians, and grips the steering wheel until his fingers hurt. He feels guilty when he leaves for work and guilty when he returns home safely. He wants relief from the memories, but another part of him believes he does not deserve relief. In session, he speaks softly at first, then with sudden intensity, as if each detail has been waiting under pressure. What stays with him is not only the image of the injured man in the road, but the sense that his own life divided there too, into a before and an after that he has not yet been able to join back together.
